result.summary: At a feast after Achilles kills Cygnus, the Greeks marvel at his invulnerability, and Nestor tells of Cæneus, a girl changed into an invulnerable man by Neptune. He describes the brawl between Centaurs and Lapithæ at Pirithoüs' wedding, ending with Cæneus buried under trees and turning into a bird.

scenes.title: Feast and Nestor's promise
scenes.summary: After a truce, Achilles sacrifices to Pallas and the chiefs feast and talk of Cygnus. Nestor says he saw Cæneus, born a woman, and Achilles asks for the story.

scenes.title: Cænis becomes Cæneus
scenes.summary: Nestor tells how Neptune violated Cænis and granted her wish to become an invulnerable man.
scenes.stakes: Cænis suffers violence and wishes never to be vulnerable to it again.

scenes.title: Wedding of Pirithoüs erupts
scenes.summary: Eurytus, drunk, seizes the bride Hippodame. Theseus rescues her and kills Eurytus with a bowl.
scenes.stakes: Hippodame is carried off and the wedding guests risk bloodshed.

scenes.title: The battle of Lapithæ and Centaurs
scenes.summary: Centaurs and Lapithæ fight with furniture, trees and brands. Many die, including Aphidas, Petræus and Dorylas.
scenes.stakes: Lives of the Lapithæ and Centaurs in a brutal brawl.

scenes.title: Cyllarus and Hylonome
scenes.summary: Beautiful Cyllarus is killed and his mate Hylonome dies on the weapon. Nestor tells of his own kills and his scar.
scenes.stakes: Lovers' lives; Hylonome chooses death with Cyllarus.

scenes.title: Latreus taunts Cæneus
scenes.summary: Nestor lists other deeds. Latreus mocks Cænis as a woman, and Cæneus wounds him while no weapon harms Cæneus.
scenes.stakes: Cæneus's identity and life are mocked and attacked.

scenes.title: Cæneus buried and made a bird
scenes.summary: The Centaurs pile trees on Cæneus, who vanishes as a bird that Mopsus hails. The Lapithæ avenge him.
scenes.stakes: Cæneus is smothered under a mountain of trees.

alias_notes.explanation: The bride is called both names in the section.

notable_quotes.reason: Latreus's taunt that Cæneus is always Cænis, a woman.
Mopsus hails the bird as Cæneus, glory of the Lapithæ.
Gendered insult telling Cæneus to take up the distaff.

analysis.text: Violence erupts from drink and lust at a feast that should honour hospitality and marriage. The nested tale shows Nestor's role as veteran storyteller.
Cæneus's transformation links gender, invulnerability and metamorphosis; the hero is finally overcome only by weight, then escapes as a bird.

legacy.text: The battle of Lapiths and Centaurs became a standard emblem of civilization against barbarism, notably in the Parthenon metopes.

fun_facts.text: The ancient Greek version of Caeneus, a Lapith who is a transformed woman, appears also in Virgil's Aeneid underworld, where Caenis is again female.

language_notes.text: Pallas is a name for Minerva (the Greek Athena), here the goddess receiving Achilles' sacrifice.
Fillets are ribbons or headbands; sacrificial animals were decked with them before being killed.
"The sacred rites had their share" means the gods' portion was offered first; the remaining meat was then eaten by the diners.
"Grandson of Æacus" is a patronymic-style title for Achilles, whose father Peleus was Æacus' son.
Perrhæbean means from Perrhæbia in Thessaly; Othrys is a Thessalian mountain, placing Cæneus in northern Greece.
"The wisdom of our age" praises Nestor as the wisest man of his generation, famed for long life and counsel.
Achilles is addressed because Nestor is telling this story to him; Thessaly was Achilles' homeland, so Cænis was his countrywoman.
Peleus married the sea-goddess Thetis, Achilles' mother. Nestor means Peleus was already promised to her, so he could not woo Cænis.
"Atracian" means of Atrax, a Thessaly town; here it refers to Cæneus, formerly Cænis, as a Thessalian.
The "cloud-born monsters" are the Centaurs, said to descend from Ixion's union with a cloud shaped like Juno.
"Hæmonian" means Thessalian, from Hæmonia, an old name for Thessaly.
"The halls smoke with the fires" refers to altar and torch fires burning at the wedding ceremony.
An omen "well nigh falsified": calling the groom fortunate nearly proved wrong because the brawl almost cost him his bride.
"Double-limbed" describes Centaurs, half man and half horse; the number [28] is the translator's footnote marker.
Tartarus is the deepest region of the underworld; here it stands for the realm of the dead generally.
Thessalian witches were said to pull the moon down from the sky with spells; this is the "incantations" reference.
A votive stag's antlers were hung on a tree as an offering to a god.
The Styx is the river of the underworld; Phorbas mocks the sleeper by saying he will drink death instead of wine.
Pallas is Minerva (Athena), who protects Theseus; the narrator adds that Theseus himself wanted people to think so.
The son of Æacus is Peleus, later father of Achilles; "thy father" is addressed to Achilles by the narrator Nestor.
Nestor is speaking to the Greeks, addressing the dead centaur Cyllarus directly. The bracketed words are the translator's additions, and the 'monstrous nature' is his half-horse body.
Castor, one of the Dioscuri, was famed as a horse-tamer. Nestor means that with a horse's neck and head Cyllarus would suit a god's steed.
The Pagasæan wood refers to the region around Pagasæ in Thessaly, the centaurs' homeland, whose streams she bathes in.
A 'yoke' of oxen is a pair, so the trunk would be too heavy for four oxen.
Nestor points to his scar as proof, as if he were showing it to his audience while telling the story.
Nestor, the narrator, wishes he had fought at Troy against Hector; he was too old by then, though in youth he fought the Centaurs.
"Two-formed" describes Centaurs, half man and half horse. Pyretus is one of them, killed by Periphas, a Lapith.
Pelethronian means from Pelethronium, a Thessalian region associated with Centaurs. A crowbar here is an improvised iron lever used as a weapon.
Mopsus was a seer (prophet) among the Lapiths, so the speaker stresses that he was also a fighter.
Emathian means Macedonian, from Emathia, a region of northern Greece.
Cænis was originally a woman, transformed into the invulnerable man Cæneus by Neptune after he assaulted her. Latreus mockingly uses her old name.
Distaff and wool baskets were symbols of women's work in spinning, so Latreus insults Cæneus's manhood.
The comparison shows how weapons bounce off Cæneus: hail on a roof, a pebble on a drum.
Cæneus was born the woman Cænis and changed into an invulnerable man by Neptune. Monychus means that the Centaurs are now what Cæneus once was, unmanly.
The Centaurs descend from Ixion, who tried to seduce Juno; Jove deceived him with a cloud, and from it the Centaurs were born.
Othrys and Pelion are mountains in Thessaly, home of the Centaurs and Lapithæ. Both were stripped of trees for the attack.
Tartarus is the deepest part of the underworld, where the wicked are punished.
The son of Ampycus is the seer Mopsus, a Lapith prophet. The speaker, Nestor, is telling the story.
Lapithæan means of the Lapithæ, the Thessalian people fighting the Centaurs.

context_notes.text: The Trojan War setting: Phrygian walls are Troy's, and the Argive trenches guard the Greek camp. Cygnus had just been killed by Achilles.
Nestor, king of Pylos, is the oldest Greek leader at Troy and is known for long stories about the past.
Cæneus was born the nymph Cænis; Neptune changed her into an invulnerable man after assaulting her, as the summary notes.
Nestor, the aged king of Pylos, is the speaker. He is famous for his long life and his long reminiscences.
Neptune, god of the sea, often appears in myth violating mortal women, then granting them a favor.
Centaurs, half-man and half-horse, were proverbially wild, especially when drunk. Eurytus is one of their leaders.
Theseus, hero-king of Athens, was Pirithoüs' close friend and is present as a guest.
The fight began at the wedding feast of Pirithoüs when a drunken Centaur tried to carry off the bride; the Lapithæ are Pirithoüs's people.
Hercules later fought and killed Nessus with poisoned arrows, so Dryas's remark foretells that fate.
The son of Ixion is Pirithoüs, king of the Lapithæ; the Centaurs were also descended from Ixion.
The son of Ægeus is Theseus, the Athenian hero and friend of Pirithoüs.
The Lapithæan house is the palace of Pirithous, king of the Lapiths, where the centaurs' drunken attack on the wedding feast began the battle.
Phonolenus's son is the centaur Phonolenus's son Hylonome is not meant; the victim is a centaur whom Nestor names only by his father.
Nestor says 'thy sire' to Achilles, whose father Peleus was also at the battle and could confirm the account.
Cæneus, a Lapith, is invulnerable, and in this battle he kills many Centaurs. Nestor is recounting the fight between Lapiths and Centaurs at Pirithous's wedding.
Latreus is a Centaur, here displaying his arms by galloping in circles.
Cæneus is called Elateïan as the son of Elatus, a Lapith. Neptune had made him invulnerable.
Ida is a mountain (probably the one in Crete or Troy). Its shaking is compared to the heaving pile of trees.

literary_notes.text: The repeated "no" lists the absent entertainments, emphasizing that war talk alone fills the night.
The narrator asks what else Achilles could discuss, implying that warriors naturally talk of battle and honor their greatest hero.
Naming Achilles by his grandfather gives him heroic stature while the Greeks wonder at Cygnus.
Nestor's hint about Cæneus' birth as a woman sets up the story of transformation to come.
Nestor's boast of two hundred years reinforces his familiar role as the aged, authoritative storyteller.
The changed voice quietly signals the completed transformation before the narrator states it.
Nestor turns to address Eurytus directly, heightening the drama and condemnation of his drunken lust.
The chaos is compared to a captured city, suggesting the scale of the violence and the sack of the wedding.
The bowl is huge and Theseus is huger still, exaggerating his heroic strength.
Objects made for feasting become weapons, turning the celebration into slaughter.
Comparing the chandelier blow to a sacrificial axe killing a bull links the violence to ritual killing.
The hissing of blood in the wound is compared to a smith quenching hot iron, a vivid and homely image.
The narrator addresses the dead or fighting Dryas directly, heightening the drama of his turn of fortune.
Aphidas sleeps through the uproar and dies unaware, a bleakly ironic end for a drinker.
The gruesome detail of Dorylas trampling his own entrails closes the episode with grotesque horror.
Gold repeated in beard and hair makes Cyllarus's youthful beauty vivid before his death.
His body is compared to applauded statues, praising his human half as if it were artistic perfection.
Repeating 'together' stresses the couple's unity and prepares for their shared death.
Hylonome's suicide on the weapon that killed him makes the lovers' devotion tragic and moving.
Brains pouring out are compared to curdled milk and liquid through a sieve, a homely image that makes the gore grotesque.
Latreus insists Cæneus is a woman, yet the "woman" cannot be wounded by him. His taunt will be answered by Cæneus's strength.
Two homely images, hail on a roof and a pebble on a drum, make Cæneus's invulnerability vivid.
Comparing Cæneus's body to struck marble emphasizes his hardness; the splintering blade shows the failure of Latreus's attack.
Vivid physical detail of the sweating, straining hero buried under oaks makes the burial tangible before the miracle.
The heaving woodpile is compared to a mountain shaken by earthquakes, conveying Cæneus's immense strength.
Nestor intrudes as eyewitness, saying he saw the bird only once, which lends the metamorphosis credibility.
Mopsus addresses the transformed Cæneus directly, turning the change into a solemn tribute to his former greatness.
